[Problem]{.card-kicker} **Sum of Beauty of All Substrings** [LC 1781 · Sum of Beauty of All Substrings](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-beauty-of-all-substrings/){difficulty="Medium"}

This is the odd one out in the chapter. Everything so far has been a *contribution swap*: take a sum over windows and re-index it as a sum over elements, each credited with the number of windows covering it (@sec-cnt-a1). Here that swap is not available. Beauty is $\max - \min$ of a histogram, and neither extreme is linear — extend a window by one character and the maximum may or may not move, while the minimum can jump when a *new* letter arrives. There is no per-cell number you can multiply by a cover count. So the answer is not to find a cleverer formula but to make the *per-window* cost $O(1)$: keep the histogram alive while the window changes, and read its extremes cheaply. That is the frequency-table maintenance of @sec-sw-p5 and @sec-ds pointed at a counting problem, and @sec-cnt-a5 is the lesson that frames it.

Two loops give each left end its own histogram, and the right end only ever walks forward — so the histogram is updated by a single increment per step instead of being rebuilt. The cost is then dominated by *reading* it: scanning $26$ cells for $\max$ and $\min$ makes each window $O(|\Sigma|)$ work, i.e. $O(n^2 \cdot 26)$, which at $n = 500$ is $\binom{501}{2} = 125{,}250$ substrings times $26 = 3{,}256{,}500$ cell reads. Comfortable, and the version to write first.

The "least frequent character" clause is where the bugs live. It means the letter whose count is smallest *among letters present* — a substring's beauty never involves a letter that does not occur in it. Read literally over a $26$-cell array, the minimum is $0$ whenever fewer than $26$ distinct letters appear, i.e. almost always; the answer then silently becomes "sum of the maximum frequency", and on `"aabcb"` that reads $21$ instead of $5$. Rung 2 filters to positive cells; rung 3 must make the same distinction through its cursor, which is why the frequency buckets are indexed from $1$.

Rung 3 kills the $26$-scan. Count the *frequencies*: `how[f]` = how many letters currently occur exactly $f$ times. Then the maximum frequency present is a cursor `maxf`, and the minimum is a cursor `minf`, and a single character increment moves each of them by at most one step (`maxf` can only rise, because a letter leaving the top bucket lands one bucket higher). The invariant that makes this airtight is that **occupied frequency buckets have no gaps**: the first letter arrives at frequency $1$, and thereafter any letter leaving bucket $f$ immediately occupies bucket $f+1$. So `minf` never has to search — if the bucket it points at empties, `minf + 1` is occupied by construction. Work per window drops to $O(1)$ amortised: $125{,}250$ steps total, and the same $O(n^2)$ shape is the best you can do because there are that many substrings to charge.

Hand-check against the storyboard, whose rows are exactly the beauties of $s[i .. j]$ as $j$ runs to the end. From left $0$: `"a"` and `"aa"` are uniform (beauty $0$, since $\max = \min$), while `"aab"`, `"aabc"`, `"aabcb"` have $\max = 2$, $\min = 1$ — charges $[0, 0, 1, 1, 1]$, $+3$. The four remaining left ends add $1 + 1 + 0 + 0$, and $3 + 1 + 1 = 5$.

Size of the answer: beauty is at most $($window length $- 1)$, hence at most $499$, and there are $125{,}250$ windows, so the total is under $499 \times 125{,}250 = 62{,}499{,}750$ — an `int` with a factor of $34$ to spare. The bound is deliberately loose: the all-uniform string `"a" * 500` scores $0$, because every one of its substrings has $\max = \min$. No modulus anywhere in this problem.
